text: The stock market is one of the few places where ordinary people can still feel that they have a chance to
change their lives. All you need is a smartphone, a trading account, and a few taps to enter the game. For
many young people, this feels almost like their last realistic opportunity to close the wealth gap. But, as we've already said
big opportunities often come with big risks. With margin trading, those risks become even larger: gains can be bigger, but losses
can come much faster. The second underlying factor is a famous concept called the 'Korea discount.' Investors use this term to
describe the tendency for South Korean stocks to trade at lower valuations than comparable businesses in other developed countries. Part of
the explanation lies in the structure of South Korea's family-controlled conglomerates, known as chaebols. Another part comes from longstanding controversies over
the rights of minority shareholders. What matters here is that many investors believe this discount exists. And if people don't believe
the market will adequately reward them for holding stocks over the long term, they become more inclined to chase profits from
shorter market swings. The third factor is short selling. In theory, short selling is a perfectly normal tool in financial markets
It helps identify irrational prices and limits the extent to which stocks become overvalued. But in the eyes of many South
Korean retail investors, short selling is a game played by large institutions, especially foreign funds. Years of scandals involving short-selling practices
have only deepened that suspicion. And when trust in the fairness of the market declines, people become less interested in playing
the long game. They want to make money quickly before they become the people someone else profits from. Finally, and perhaps
most importantly, investing has simply become too easy. Never before in history has betting on the market been so convenient
In the past, if you wanted to trade stocks, you had to call a broker, wait for confirmation, and pay substantial
fees. Now everything is right there on your phone. Buying takes seconds. Selling takes seconds. On top of that, financial content
is everywhere: analysis videos, livestreams, online communities, forums, news reports, recommendations, and predictions. Every day, people are repeatedly told that there
is another opportunity in the market. This stock is about to surge! A new trend is forming! Another rally is coming
everyone! When all these things come together, the market starts looking more like a social network than a place to invest
